Abstract: Pyrolysis technology has become a hot issue in the industry of harmless 28 treatment of sludge in recent years. The present ectopic catalytic pyrolysis process 29 suffers from the defects of unidirectional flow of pyrolysis steam, poor heating value 30 of the output heavy tar, which is difficult to be reutilized, etc. In this paper, we design 31 a cyclic catalytic cracking by pyrolytic steam process to optimize the above defects: 32 under the optimal experimental conditions (pyrolysis starting temperature was 500 ℃, 33 final temperature was 800 ℃, iron-based carbon catalyst dosage was 4 g, and motor 34 speed was 1050 r/min), this process generated more pyrolysis gas and light tar. The 35 cyclic catalytic cracking by pyrolytic steam process could increase the residence time 36 of pyrolysis steam in the reaction unit and promoted the secondary cracking, catalytic 37 and reforming effects of tar. 38 Keywords: Sludge; Pyrolysis; Cyclic catalytic cracking; Secondary cracking; Tar 39 Preprint not peer reviewed

Sewage sludge is the solid residue from wastewater treatment, and nowadays, the sludge production is increasing. In China, sludge production is expected to be

˃9.7

×

10 7

tons in 2023 [1]. Harmful components found in sludge, including heavy metals, pathogenic microorganism [2], and various toxic and harmful organic substances,

serious impact on human health and living environment [3]. Therefore, it is necessary to pre-treat the sludge before its resourceful disposal or utilization to avoid potential

risks of secondary pollution to the environment and human health due to improper treatment [3].

Therefore, sludge need to be treated with appropriate processes, for example:

anaerobic digestion, aerobic composting and thermochemical treatment to eliminate the potential for environmental pollution [4]. Anaerobic digestion is an economically

and environmentally friendly method that converts organic matter into biogas in the absence of oxygen [5, 6]. However, the resulting high osmotic pressure and inhibition

of the microorganisms by high salinity limit the development of anaerobic biological treatment technologies [7, 8]. Aerobic composting process has low energy

consumption, low odor generation rate, and can produce organic fertilizer products with certain added value and no harm [9]. Usually supplementary materials or

microbial agents are added to the compost pile to optimize the composting effect [10].

However, the purchase of auxiliary materials and microbial agents increases the cost of composting and there are risks in the use of bacterial culture [11]. Although

40 1. Introduction Preprint not peer reviewed

|   61 | anaerobic digestion and aerobic composting are the technologies traditionally                                   |
|------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|   62 | employed to treat sludge, recent research has found that thermochemical technologies                            |
|   63 | that can further improve energy efficiency [12]. Nowadays, the main technologies for                            |
|   64 | the thermochemical treatment of sludge include gasification, incineration and                                   |
|   65 | pyrolysis.                                                                                                      |
|   66 | The advantage of gasification disposal technology is that it converts sludge into a                             |
|   67 | mixture of CO, H2, CH4 and combustible gaseous hydrocarbons [13]. However, the                                  |
|   68 | tar produced during the gasification process can cause many problems with the                                   |
|   69 | product gas, such as clogging of downstream piping, valves and injector jets [14].                              |
|   70 | Incineration disposal technology is used extensively and can completely break                                   |
|   71 | pathogens and organic contaminants [15, 16], high degree of non-hazardous, but                                  |
|   72 | incineration needs to provide auxiliary fuel and can't achieve the effect of zero waste                         |
|   73 | emissions, so the need to think about flue gas cleaning and fly ash treatment [17].                             |
|   74 | Compared with sludge gasification and sludge incineration, sludge pyrolysis is the                              |
|   75 | preferred technology due to its high volume reduction rate, low pollutant gas                                   |
|   76 | emission, self-sufficiency in energy and high resource recovery rate [18]. Pyrolysis                            |
|   77 | products include H2, CO and CH4, which can be used as fuel; tar can be used as liquid                           |
|   78 | fuel and chemical reagent raw material; bio-char has rich pore structure and can be  Preprint not peer reviewed |
|   79 | used to make functional materials (soil conditioner, adsorbent, catalyst, etc.) [19].                           |
|   80 | Sludge pyrolysis technology has the advantages of reduction, non-hazardous and                                  |
|   81 | resourcefulness [18] and has become one of the most promising disposal methods for                              |

|   82 | sludge. In addition, pyrolysis technology enables more than 50% of the carbon in        |
|------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|   83 | dewatered sludge to be sequestered, which also has positive significance in promoting   |
|   84 | "carbon peaking" and "carbon neutral".                                                  |
|   85 | Currently the most important sludge pyrolysis technology is sludge catalytic            |
|   86 | pyrolysis [20, 21]. In sludge catalytic pyrolysis methods, depending on the feedstock   |
|   87 | and catalyst configuration, they can be divided into in-situ catalysis (where pyrolysis |
|   88 | and catalysis occur simultaneously in a single reactor) and ex-situ catalysis (where    |
|   89 | catalytic reforming of pyrolysis steam (PS) occurs in a second reactor section). Some   |
|   90 | research has shown that in-situ catalytic pyrolysis may reduce the contact of PS with   |
|   91 | the catalyst and that coke buildup tends to form on the catalyst surface, leading to    |
|   92 | problems of reduced catalytic activity [22] .  In order to solve the problem, some      |
|   93 | researchers have suggested that the vapor-catalyst contact reaction should be further   |
|   94 | optimized in the process of catalysis [22, 23] . However, the tar produced by the       |
|   95 | catalytic reaction cannot be completely cracked because the catalytic cracking time is  |
|   96 | too short, leads to the production of heavy tar. And the coalesced tar may polymerize   |
|   97 | to form more complex compounds, making its removal more difficult [24] .  It was        |
|   98 | assumed that a technology could extend the catalytic time, increase the residence time  |
|   99 | of PS in the reactor, thereby reducing the complex organic matter content of the coke   |

100 and increasing the yield of pyrolysis gas (PG) to bio-char. But there are less relevant 101 studies. 102 Therefore, in order to increase the reaction time of sludge pyrolysis, the cyclic Preprint not peer reviewed

|   103 | catalytic cracking by pyrolytic steam (CCCPS) process was designed in this study.                                  |
|-------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|   104 | The main evaluation indexes are pyrolysis product yield, PG fraction, and lower                                    |
|   105 | heating value (LHV). In this research process, we debug the different influencing                                  |
|   106 | factors such as pyrolysis temperature, iron-based carbon catalyst (IBCC) dosage, and                               |
|   107 | motor speed rate in this process, and also analyzed the nature of sludge pyrolysis                                 |
|   108 | products (PG, tar, and bio-char). The mechanism of the CCCPS process was clarified                                 |
|   109 | by comparing with ectopic catalytic pyrolysis (ECP) process, and the feasibility of the                            |
|   110 | process was also explored. This process proposes a new sludge resourceful disposal                                 |
|   111 | technology based on catalytic reforming of pyrolysis steam cycle. The process                                      |
|   112 | realized safe and harmless sludge disposal and efficient resource utilization, providing                           |
|   113 | new insights and reference basis to sludge pyrolysis resourceful disposal technology.                              |

|   210 | 3.Results and discussion                                                                                     |
|   211 | 3.1 Effect of temperature on sludge pyrolysis products                                                       |
|   212 | Fig.1A shows the percentage distribution of pyrolysis products at different                                  |
|   213 | pyrolysis temperatures. With the increase of pyrolysis temperature, the yield of bio-                        |
|   214 | char and tar showed a decreasing trend, while the yield of PG gradually increased.                           |
|   215 | When the pyrolysis temperature was 800 °C, the bio-char, PG, and tar yields were                             |
|   216 | (54.55 ± 1.34) wt.%, (20.94 ± 1.47) wt.%, and (24.42 ± 1.62) wt.%, respectively. This                        |
|   217 | result shows that at high temperature pyrolysis conditions can promote the production                        |
|   218 | of PG and reduce the yield of bio-char and tar, which is similar to the results of Tao                       |
|   219 | Kan et al [28]. This may be due to the fact that the high temperature promoted the                           |
|   220 | secondary cracking of the tar and enhanced the catalytic reforming reaction of the PS                        |
|   221 | in contact with the bio-char. In addition, the coke yield in the tar increased from                          |
|   222 | (0.016 ± 0.006) wt.% to (0.067 ± 0.004) wt.% under high temperature environment,                             |
|   223 | which may be caused by the partial coking of the tar under high temperature                                  |
|   224 | conditions [24, 29].                                                                                         |
|   225 | Fig.1B and 1C show the effect of different temperatures in the pyrolysis and                                 |
|   226 | catalytic cycle sections on the distribution of PG components. Fig.1B shows that  Preprint not peer reviewed |
|   227 | during the pyrolysis ramping up process, the PG yield increased with increasing                              |
|   228 | pyrolysis temperature when the pyrolysis final temperature was 600 °C, and the PG                            |

|   229 | yields reached a maximum of (51.12 ± 0.34) wt.% and (37.03 ± 0.54) wt.% at                                         |
|-------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|   230 | pyrolysis temperatures of 600 °C and 500 °C, respectively, when the pyrolysis final                                |
|   231 | temperature was 700 °C and 800 °C. However, the effect on PG yield was not                                         |
|   232 | significant when the pyrolysis section temperature was kept at 800°C with final                                    |
|   233 | pyrolysis temperatures of 700 and 800  ℃.  This shows that the increase in temperature                             |
|   234 | of the catalytic section and the external circulation section (same as the pyrolysis end                           |
|   235 | temperature) promotes the secondary cracking of the tar produced by the sludge                                     |
|   236 | pyrolysis and generates more PG [30, 31]. This is supported by the increase in the                                 |
|   237 | content of the collected PG components from (12.56 ± 0.42) wt.% to (51.12 ± 0.34)                                  |
|   238 | wt.% with the increase in the pyrolysis end temperature when the pyrolysis                                         |
|   239 | temperature is the similar 500 °C.                                                                                 |
|   240 | Fig.1C shows the total amount of each component produced by sludge pyrolysis.                                      |
|   241 | As the pyrolysis end temperature condition increases, the yield of H2 increases rapidly                            |
|   242 | from (34.33 ± 5) wt.% to (90.53 ± 7) wt.%, the yield of CO increases from (16.6 ±                                  |
|   243 | 1.5) wt.% to (58.25 ± 3.5) wt.%, and CH4 increases from (19.32 ± 2) wt.% to (45.83 ±                               |
|   244 | 4.5) wt.%. There are two possible reasons for these results. As the temperature of the  Preprint not peer reviewed |
|   245 | pyrolysis section increases, more PG is generated by the direct cracking of certain                                |
|   246 | organic substances in the sludge [19]. Based on this CCCPS process, the volatile                                   |
|   247 | substances generated by pyrolysis can circulate in the process, which allows these                                 |
|   248 | volatile substances to stay longer in the high temperature zone and promotes the re-                               |
|   249 | cracking of these substances by heat to produce H2, CO and CH4, according to                                       |

According to Table.S4, the organic compounds in sludge tar can be divided into oxygen-containing compounds, nitrogen-containing compounds, hydrocarbons,

sulfur-containing compounds, and a few other compounds (including compounds containing elements such as chlorine, bromine, silicon and phosphorus), among which

hydrocarbons account for the highest proportion, especially aromatics, which account for 67.94% of the organic phase of tar in CCCPS process and 62.83% in ECP process

accounting for 62.83%. It shows that the cyclization of organic matter in the PS is enhanced during the cyclic catalytic pyrolysis of sludge. This may be caused by the

prolonged PS residence time in the CCCPS process, which is similar to the study by
